name: Colin Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms or political groups. This is confidential. What does your working week look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach eight violin pupils on Mondays, conduct the church choir on Sundays, and lead a quartet at community concerts. My master's degree in music helped me earn these posts, but learning the town's singers took years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the money side like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The pay is ordinary for a musician, and I've saved about four months of expenses. There are some teaching posts nearby, though I would rather keep the families and choir I know.

say: I'd say **choir singing** and quartet work still turn on people listening together.
I'd accept **tidier records** without changing how I teach or rehearse.
think: My **four-month reserve** and regular lessons make a small change manageable.
The **autumn calendar** matters more to me than a tool I don't use.
do: Keep my **eight pupils**, quartet rehearsal and Sunday choir work.
Put spare **concert money** into savings after household bills are paid.
feel: I feel **calm** about income, while watching autumn concert dates.
S0.quote: A choir cannot file its way into singing in tune.
fieldNote: His **regular fees** support a calm mood despite seasonal concerts and some uncertain bookings.
He avoids **AI tools** even when their routine savings would be harmless.

steps.text: Keep eight pupils and Sunday choir sessions
Put spare concert fees into savings after bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the choir and the quartet that a better filing system is fine, but the singer still has to take a breath with the room. I wouldn't make a speech about AI if it stayed small. A choir cannot file its way into singing in tune.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't use those tools and don't intend to for a saved minute. My teaching and Sunday choir fees are steady, and I've put aside about four months of expenses; I still keep an eye on the autumn concert bookings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the Monday violin lessons, Thursday quartet rehearsal and Sunday choir. Each month this year, I'll put part of the concert money in savings if the household bills are paid first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm enough. The usual worry is a thin concert calendar, but the lessons and choir have carried me through quiet months before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when a concert was cancelled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The community hall cancelled an October concert last year. The choir fee and eight regular pupils covered the bills, and I didn't need to draw down the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you secure the next hall date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would talk to the hall manager face to face before our next autumn date. I prefer a written date afterward, even when the person is an old friend.

say: I'd ask **venues** to be clear when paid arrangements become software work.
I'd insist on a **fair fee** for the rehearsal and playing we still do.
think: **Copying and planning** could lose value before robot players appear.
A **fifth of my pay** may go even if lessons and choir work hold.
do: List this year's **copying fees** and seek a written choir contract now.
Offer **two lesson slots** if families commit for a term after fees fall.
Cancel the **second rehearsal room** if copying income goes.
feel: I feel **anxious** about quiet income loss, reluctant to show it at rehearsal.
S1.quote: A week's groceries can disappear one copied score at a time.
fieldNote: He sees **small screen tasks** threatened first despite confidence in human lessons.
His extra **lesson slots** need term commitments; he will not rent a room on verbal interest.

steps.text: List paid copying fees and request a written choir contract
Offer two lesson slots if families commit for a term
Cancel the second rehearsal room if copying income disappears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the quartet that venues should say plainly when they replace paid arrangements with software. I wouldn't scold a client for saving money, but I would insist on a fair fee for the work we actually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the small scores I copy and the rehearsal plans I write to lose value first. That could take a fifth of my pay before robots ever come near a stage; lessons and choir work might hold, but I cannot be sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll list the paid copying jobs and ask the choir committee for next year's written contract. If those fees fall during the first year, I'll offer two more violin lesson slots at the church room, but only if families commit to a term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, and I dislike saying it out loud to the quartet. Four months saved helps, but I don't want to spend it merely because the small jobs quietly vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the lost copying work mean in money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month I copied parts for a local concert and earned enough to cover a week's groceries. If that work goes, I'd stop paying for a second rehearsal room before I cut the pupils' lesson time. A week's groceries can disappear one copied score at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want more lessons but dislike new tools; how does that fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I won't use AI to teach a child how to hold a bow. I can teach two more pupils myself if their families want weekly work, but I won't reserve a room for promises.

say: I'd ask the **choir** to sign future dates before 2028.
I'd keep the **quartet** practising for people who still want live players.
think: **AGI in 2028** could replace scores and feedback before robots arrive around 2031.
My **four-month reserve** would not sustain years of falling lesson income.
do: Seek a **two-year choir agreement** and count term payments this week.
Apply for a **school tutor post** after 2028 if four families leave and a vacancy opens.
Cut **concert travel** if four pupils leave while seeking replacement work.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by a short route from lost lessons to depleted savings.
S2.quote: Four months of savings is not four years of work.
fieldNote: He understands **thinking AI** can cut income three years before robot players arrive.
The **school application** depends on four lost pupils and a real vacancy; he would keep choir work until offered a post.

steps.text: Seek two-year choir agreement; keep choir until a school offers paid work
Apply for advertised school tutor vacancies after 2028 if four pupils leave
Cut concert travel if four pupils leave

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the choir committee that 2028 is soon and we should sign next season's dates now. I would still ask the quartet to practise, because the audience deserves actual players.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full AGI in 2028 could write scores, plan rehearsals and give pupils feedback more cheaply than I can. Robot performers would follow around 2031, but the fifth of my income from copying and planning could go first, and families might question lessons too. Four months of savings is not four years of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this week I'll ask the choir committee for a two-year teaching and conducting agreement and count each pupil's term payments. In the first year after 2028, if four families leave, I'll apply for the open music tutor post at the nearby school; I won't resign from the choir unless I get an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed by how little time there is to replace regular pay. I won't pretend a signed agreement can stop every change, but it would let me sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the nearby school job really available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The nearby school advertised a tutor vacancy last spring and filled it, so I don't know if another will open. I'd ask to be told about future posts, but I wouldn't bank on one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would four lost pupils mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If four families go, that is roughly half the lesson income. I would take the school application seriously and cut concert travel until something is signed.

say: I'd tell **parents** I will keep teaching while the value of lessons changes.
I'd use **five years** to strengthen the choir and local ensembles.
think: **AGI in 2031** threatens scores and tutoring before robots arrive around 2034.
Losing **copying fees** would hurt, but a longer warning helps me build live work.
do: Propose a **family ensemble** next term only with a room agreement and eight paid families.
Continue the **series** after AGI only if eight families renew.
feel: I feel **anxious** about lost fees, steadier with a five-year trial.
S3.quote: I would rather teach eight real families than plan for eighty imaginary ones.
fieldNote: The **five-year runway** lets him build family music locally without changing his trade.
His **eight-family threshold** and accompanist pay make the church series conditional and accountable.

steps.text: Propose a family ensemble if eight families pay and room terms are signed
Seek a three-year choir contract before 2031
Continue the series if eight families renew after AGI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my pupils' parents that I can keep teaching through 2031, while we work out what a lesson is worth. Five years gives me time to strengthen the choir's place in the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI could write scores and tutor thinking work by 2031; robot players would come around 2034. I expect the copying fees to fade before then, but five years lets me build more live teaching and conducting work without betting the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I'll offer the church a six-month family ensemble series, but only with a signed room agreement and eight paid families. Before 2031 I'll seek a three-year choir contract; in the first year after AGI, I'll keep the series if at least eight families renew, otherwise return to individual lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about replacing that fifth of my pay, though not as frightened as with two years. A church room and parents I know make the trial less of a leap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who carries the cost of the ensemble series?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would charge families per term and pay the accompanist first. If eight don't sign, I won't launch and ask the committee to fund another concert instead. I would rather teach eight real families than plan for eighty imaginary ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you persuade the church committee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The church committee is careful with money, as it should be. I'd bring a one-page budget, not a promise that children will turn up.

say: I'd ask the **choir** to pass on the habit of singing together.
I'd favour **local teaching** over chasing tools I don't trust.
think: At **37**, retirement will not protect me when AGI arrives in 2036.
Robot players around **2039** may challenge concerts, but I can deepen in-person teaching.
do: Ask **church and school** to fund room and supervision before announcing a youth concert.
Build **six months of savings** from teaching and conducting before 2036.
Continue the **concert** after AGI only if both partners still fund it.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about paid playing, with time to grow local teaching.
S4.quote: A yearly concert cannot pay the month's bills.
fieldNote: The **ten-year warning** suits his preference for church, school and steady teaching relationships.
Written **room and supervision commitments** prevent a community concert from becoming a family bill.

steps.text: Get written church hall funding and school supervision commitments before announcing youth concert
Build six months of savings from teaching and conducting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the choir ten years is long enough to teach a new generation properly. I don't want the town to lose the habit of singing together just because sound can be made cheaply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 37 when AGI arrives in 2036, so I can't simply wait for retirement. Robots might play around 2039, and I may lose copying fees much earlier; a decade lets me deepen the teaching and choir work that people choose in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask the church and school to run a joint yearly youth concert if they both sign for room and supervision costs. Over the decade I'll build six months of savings from teaching and conducting; in the first year after 2036, I'll keep the concert only if both partners still fund it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the future of paid playing, but there is time to work through it. I would rather build a local music habit than chase a tool I don't trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the two partners have to provide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school would need a teacher in charge of the children and the church would need to cover the hall. I won't announce a date until both agree in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a yearly concert replace lessons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also keep my regular pupils because weekly lessons pay the household bills. If either partner drops out, I'll cancel rather than ask families for emergency money. A yearly concert cannot pay the month's bills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because four months of savings could run out while copying and lesson fees shrink. A signed choir agreement and a real school vacancy, if pupils leave, would give me choices without abandoning the town.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether families still want a teacher who knows their child by name. That matters to me more than any argument about machines, though I know families must mind the price.

headlineQuote: I don't want the town to lose the habit of singing together just because sound can be made cheaply.
portrait: Colin is a **27-year-old** violinist with a music master's degree, teaching eight pupils, leading a quartet and conducting church choir.
He has **four months saved** and some nearby jobs, but prefers familiar work and never uses AI tools.
He expects **scores and planning** to lose fees before robot players arrive three years after each AGI date.
He seeks **signed commitments** from families, church and school before taking on new rooms or concerts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because copying and lesson fees could shrink before he can secure replacement work.
whatWouldHelp: A signed **choir agreement** and a genuine school vacancy would give him choices if pupils leave.
